name: Open superior approach to the clavicle
corridor: Supraclavicular incision through platysma and clavipectoral fascia to the superior clavicle

positioning.text: Position beach-chair or supine with scapular support and free shoulder motion to elevate the lateral fragment during reduction.

setup.text: Prep the neck, shoulder, and arm; ensure whole-clavicle imaging and use drill stops or guarded technique to protect the deep plexus, vessels, and pleura.

surface_landmarks.text: Mark sternoclavicular and acromioclavicular joints, clavicular borders, fracture, deltoid attachment laterally, and planned superior plate span.

incision.text: Make an oblique 8–10 cm incision directly superior to and centered on the fracture, extending as needed for medial or lateral patterns.

superficial_interval.text: Raise limited anterior and posterior subcutaneous flaps, identify and preserve supraclavicular sensory branches, and open clavipectoral fascia.

deep_interval.text: Reflect only the pectoralis or deltoid attachment required for plate seating, keeping lateral deltoid as a contiguous repairable sheet and preserving fragment soft tissues.

layers.text: Skin, subcutaneous tissue, platysma and supraclavicular nerves, clavipectoral fascia and periosteum, deltoid or pectoral attachment as required, then superior clavicle.

structures_encountered.text: Platysma, supraclavicular nerves, clavipectoral fascia, pectoralis major, trapezius, deltoid laterally, periosteum, and clavicle are encountered.

structures_at_risk.text: Supraclavicular sensory branches, subclavian vessels, brachial plexus, pleura, deltoid attachment, and fragment perfusion are at risk.

danger_zones.text: Superior-to-inferior drilling points toward critical infraclavicular structures; maintain direct far-cortex control and avoid deep plunging, especially medially.

retraction_hazards.text: Do not place unprotected retractors under the clavicle or tension preserved sensory nerves; expand exposure rather than increasing deep pressure.

exposure.text: Provides direct access across lateral, shaft, and medial clavicle and a straight view for superior plate contouring and application.

limitations.text: Superior implants can be prominent beneath thin skin, and comparative evidence does not show a universal union or functional advantage over anteroinferior plating.

extensions.text: Extend along the superior clavicle, reflecting deltoid or pectoral tissue only where required and preserving AC and coracoclavicular ligament attachments when intact.

indications.text: Applicable to lateral, diaphyseal, and medial clavicle fractures selected for open reduction, with superior plating especially common for lateral patterns.

relative_contraindications.text: Consider anteroinferior or limited fixation when superior hardware prominence, scar location, compromised superior skin, or the required drill trajectory is unfavorable.

implant_implications.text: Contour the plate to the superior S-curve, obtain balanced fragment fixation, avoid AC or SC joint penetration, and use guarded bicortical drilling.

fluoroscopy_implications.text: Confirm length, alignment, rotation, articular-joint clearance, plate contour, and safe screw lengths across the entire construct.

closure.text: Repair reflected deltoid or pectoral attachments, cover the plate with clavipectoral fascia and periosteum, precisely reapproximate platysma, and close skin without tension.

complications.text: Complications include sensory numbness or neuroma, prominent hardware and removal, deep vascular or plexus injury, pneumothorax, deltoid dysfunction, infection, nonunion, and implant failure.

bailouts.text: If superior drilling cannot be protected or soft-tissue coverage is inadequate, reposition the plate anteroinferiorly or change fixation strategy rather than accepting unsafe screws or exposed hardware.

procedure_applications.condition: A lateral, shaft, or medial fracture requires direct superior exposure and superior plate fixation

questions.question: Which fractures are commonly plated superiorly?
questions.answer: Lateral clavicle fractures, although shaft and medial fractures may also use superior fixation.

questions.question: What sensory complication follows supraclavicular nerve injury?
questions.answer: Numbness or a painful proximal neuroma.

questions.question: Why avoid stripping comminuted fragments?
questions.answer: Maintaining their soft-tissue blood supply is more important than perfect reduction of every fragment.
